subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (i, 0) and (0, −i), then show that A² = −I.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Multiply A by A
steps.margin_note: First mark. A is diagonal, so each diagonal entry simply squares: i² and (−i)². Both come to −1.
steps.memory_tip: A is diagonal, so each diagonal entry simply squares: i² and (−i)².

recall.must_convey: That A² is A times A, giving i² and (−i)² on the diagonal.
accept: multiply the matrix by itself so the diagonal entries square
A squared has i squared and minus i squared on the diagonal
row into column multiplication on a diagonal matrix

steps.why: A diagonal matrix squares entry by entry — but only because the off-diagonal zeros make every cross term zero, not as a general rule.
common_mistakes: Squaring the entries without doing the multiplication.

steps.label: Use i² = −1
steps.margin_note: Second mark. i² = −1 and (−i)² = i² = −1, so both diagonal entries are −1 — which is −I.
steps.memory_tip: i² = −1 and (−i)² = i² = −1, so both diagonal entries are −1 — which is −I.

accept: i squared is minus one and minus i squared is also minus one so A squared is minus I
both diagonal entries are minus one giving minus the identity
i square minus one, so A square equals minus I
it comes to negative the identity matrix

steps.why: (−i)² = (−1)²i² = i² — the minus squares away. Both entries land on −1 for slightly different reasons.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as a grid of −1s without naming it −I.

insider_note: A is diagonal, so A² simply squares each diagonal entry. (−i)² = i² = −1 as well, which is why both entries agree and the result is −I rather than I.
